source_document.body:
Memorial University engineering interns at Trinity Performance Minerals’ mine in Conception Bay South, N.L., in 2025. Credit: Memorial University.
By: Devan Murugan November 11, 2026
ST. JOHN’S, N.L. — Memorial University is developing a master’s program in mining and mineral processing to help ease an industry skills shortage years before graduates from its planned undergraduate degree enter the workforce.
The proposed course-based degree would take 12 to 16 months, Salim Ahmed, head of process engineering at Memorial, told The Northern Miner this month.
“It will have flexibility to accommodate the need of the industry,” Ahmed said. “There will be significant demand for skilled manpower. At the same time, we’re not getting enough people, and people are retiring.”
Mining in Canada could require about 246,400 hires between 2026 and 2035 under a baseline forecast that includes replacing workers leaving the industry, the Mining Industry Human Resources Council estimates. Memorial’s first undergraduate mining engineers would not graduate for almost six years, Ahmed said, leaving a gap the shorter program could help address.
Workforce pressure
Discussions about a dedicated mining engineering program began in 2018, initially involving Vale (NYSE: VALE), and intensified over the past two years as companies became increasingly concerned about retirements and future demand for specialized workers, Ahmed said.
The master’s would complement a proposed co-operative bachelor of engineering in mining and mineral processing backed by a $9-million (US$6.4-million) initiative announced by Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham at the Mineral Resources Review conference in St. John’s on Nov. 4.
Both programs are targeting a fall 2027 intake, although the master’s could be delayed until fall 2028 depending on student recruitment, Ahmed said.
Both programs remain subject to university approval. The undergraduate proposal has cleared the engineering faculty council and is expected to go before senate and the board of regents in the coming months, Memorial said on Nov. 5.
The university wants to work directly with mining companies to identify their training needs and develop courses that allow existing employees to acquire additional skills, Ahmed said. Memorial also plans shorter microcredential courses for practising engineers and other industry professionals.
Automation and AI
The programs are being designed for an industry increasingly shaped by automation, artificial intelligence and data-driven operations.
Future mining engineers will need to understand technologies ranging from autonomous equipment to predictive maintenance systems capable of identifying machinery deterioration before failures occur, Ahmed said.
Rather than treating artificial intelligence as a separate subject, Ahmed wants data analytics and emerging technologies integrated throughout the curriculum.
The approach would build on conventional engineering fundamentals, including thermodynamics, fluid mechanics and equipment design, while incorporating modern applications.
He compared the approach with changes in engineering safety education, where safety principles have increasingly been integrated across courses rather than confined to a single module.
The aim is to produce engineers who understand both the physical processes involved in mining and the digital systems increasingly used to manage them.
Industry backing
The undergraduate initiative is supported by $3.9 million from Vale Base Metals, a unit of Vale, which will also provide future co-operative work placements.
Memorial is contributing about $2.8 million in in-kind support, while the provincial government is providing $2.25 million through the Canada–Newfoundland and Labrador Labour Market Development Agreement.
The funding will support faculty recruitment, curriculum development, laboratory preparation and student recruitment.
Of the 47 courses required for the undergraduate program, 36 are already offered, allowing it to build on existing engineering expertise, Memorial says.
The university intends to introduce the remaining courses and laboratories as students progress through the degree, with resources allocated over seven years, Ahmed said.
Specialized courses
That approach gives the university time to prepare specialized upper-year courses while initially concentrating on the first cohort of students.
Mining accounts for about 9% of Newfoundland and Labrador’s gross domestic product, the provincial government said in its 2026 economic outlook. The province forecasts about 9,200 person-years of employment in mining and exploration in 2026.
Mineral exploration spending is forecast to reach a record $283.3 million in 2026, according to the provincial government.
Wakeham pointed to opportunities in new mines, mineral processing and critical minerals development, while warning that the province’s mining ambitions were already running ahead of its available workforce.
“Quite simply, the opportunities ahead of us are bigger than our current workforce.”

This 1986 Blue Bird Wanderlodge Still Delivers High-End Motorhome Living Thanks to $110K Renovation
27 photos
Photo: Collecting Cars
Long before today’s luxury motorhomes that feel like rolling homes on wheels, American manufacturers were already crafting some remarkable, opulent recreational vehicles. One of these manufacturers was Blue Bird Corporation, and its most remarkable RV creation was the Wanderlodge, a high-end motorhome aimed at an elite clientele.
When hearing the name Blue Bird, most people think of those iconic yellow school buses, but the US manufacturer has produced a wide variety of other vehicle types, including transit buses, mobile libraries, mobile police command centers, and even motorhomes.
Combining the rugged, durable foundation of a heavy-duty bus with the kind of interior amenities expected in a high-end residence, the Wanderlodge was one of the most luxurious motorhomes of its time, with its pricing comparable with the cost of a medium-sized house.
Initially introduced in 1963 as the Transit Home, this Class A RV was produced by Blue Bird through its Cardinal Manufacturing subsidiary in Fort Valley, Georgia, from 1963 to 2008. It was renamed the Wanderlodge, from mixing the words wanderlust and lodge, in 1968, and it spanned three generations, transitioning from gas-powered front-engine models to powerful rear-engine diesel units, and eventually introducing slide-out expansions in the late 1990s.
Photo: Collecting Cars What’s important to note is that, even though it’s based on Blue Bird’s heavy-duty All American commercial and school bus platform, the Wanderlodge is not a converted school bus . It was envisioned and produced as a luxury Class A recreational vehicle from the get-go, and unlike other mass-produced RVs, it was assembled largely by hand and offered a customizable interior, with over 200 options to choose from for floor plans, cabinetry, appliances, upholstery, and more.
Throughout the 45-year production run, Blue Bird continually refined the motorhome, which was offered in lengths raging from 31 feet (9.4 meters) to 45 feet (13.7 meters). It was widely considered a pioneer and a gold standard in luxury recreational vehicles, and it attracted a select clientele, the likes of Johnny Cash, King Hussein of Jordan, and former U.S. President Jimmy Carter.
An example of the Wanderlodge is now being offered for sale in France, and it perfectly showcases why this classic American motorhome is considered by many better than some modern RVs. What we have here is a 1986 Blue Bird Wanderlodge PT38 that, according to the seller, has benefited from renovations and upgrades worth about $110,000 in recent years.
Photo: Collecting Cars These motorhomes were built with an all-steel chassis to meet school bus safety standards for roll-over protection, and this is reportedly valid for this particular unit as well. Its construction is said to incorporate galvanized steel and aviation-style riveted bodywork, making it way sturdier and more durable than you’d expect a recreational vehicle to be.
Under the hood of this Wanderlodge PT38 unit lies a 12.1-liter Detroit Diesel 8V92 two-stroke turbocharged V8 engine, producing a reported 470 hp. Power is sent to the rear wheels via an Allison four-speed automatic transmission, and the chassis integrates full air-ride suspension, full air brakes, and 22.5-inch chrome alloy wheels fitted with Toyo M170Z tires.
On the outside, it’s finished in a two-tone black and gold color scheme, with gray, red, and black decals, and is adorned with exterior fabric awnings, a full-length roof rack, and a rear access ladder. Several external storage compartments provide plenty of room for luggage and other items, while a slide-out tray holds a grill for outdoor cooking.
Photo: Collecting Cars The interior is where the Wanderlodge’s luxurious nature is more aparent. The living space has a distinct 1980s character due to the color palette dominated by creams, browns, and natural wood tones. The included amenities and choice of materials give it a residential feel, with brown and beige leatherette, beige crushed velvet upholstery, wooden flooring, wooden worktops, and gloss-white and wood veneer-covered cabinets.
The layout provides dedicated spaces for relaxation, cooking, dining, and sleeping, with a seamless flow between areas. Futon sofas at the front are great for socializing and relaxing, a dedicated booth-style dining area provides space for meals and remote work, and the large kitchen lets you cook your favorite meals on the road. There is also a proper double bed at the rear and a bathroom with a shower cabin, a toilet, a washbasin, and storage solutions.
The kitchen is particularly well equipped for a motorhome that’s 40 years old, including an over, a three-burner gas hob, a microwave, and a full-size fridge-freezer. There is also a separate wine and beer refrigerator, along with a toaster and a sink with cold and hot water. According to the listing, the kitchen and plumbing systems have undergone recent renovations.
Other amenities include electrically adjustable front seats, cruise control, a Pioneer double-DIN multimedia system, a television, a Cobra CB radio, and a gas/smoke alarm system.
Photo: Collecting Cars The motorhome is also equipped for self-sufficiency , with a 12kW Kohler generator for powering the onboard amenities. Recently installed lithium batteries with a 560Ah capacity, a Victron charger-converter, and 900 watts of solar panels add to its off-grid capabilities.
Other improvements that have been made lately include a replacement gearbox and rear axle, which were installed in 2014, ten new chassis air cushions, new tires, and a whole body repaint job.
This 1986 Blue Bird Wanderlodge PT38 RV is said to be one of only 63 examples built in this particular length, making it an unusual find, especially on the European market. It was originally registered abroad in 1986 and is now offered for sale out of La Clayette, France, via Collecting Cars.
Before getting carried away by its impressive looks and specification, there are some things worth considering. For instance, the seller notes a hydraulic leak on the lifting jack system, and though the odometer displays just 6,430 miles (10,348 km), the engine hours suggest the motorhome might have actually covered about 202,350 miles (325,650 km).

As Capricor Therapeutics awaits a pivotal decision for its embattled Duchenne muscular dystrophy cell therapy deramiocel, the biotech revealed it cut around 10% of its workforce.
Capricor had 231 fulltime employees as of Dec. 31, 2025, according to an SEC filing , meaning the layoffs may have affected around 23 individuals.
The move was made “to align our organization with our near-term priorities,” the biotech said in its third quarter earnings report on Tuesday.
Capricor is nearing a possible end to a 16-month regulatory saga. Deramiocel was rejected by the FDA in July 2025 after a planned advisory committee meeting was canceled. Then, in December last year, the company claimed that the Phase 3 HOPE-3 trial hit both its primary endpoint, showing statistically significant benefits in upper-limb function, and the secondary endpoint of slowed decline in cardiac function, as measured by left ventricular ejection fraction.

Capricor Heads Back to FDA With Pivotal Results for DMD Cardiomyopathy Therapy
Six months after receiving a surprise rejection due to what the FDA called “lack of substantial evidence of effectiveness,” Capricor’s cell therapy deramiocel showed significant benefits in upper-limb function and slowed decline in cardiac function in a Phase III trial.

However, the FDA questioned the therapy’s success on these endpoints, and an adcomm in July did not go well.
After much discussion on the FDA’s decision to base its review on an outdated statistical analysis plan, the agency’s Cellular, Tissue, and Gene Therapies Advisory Committee (CTGTAC) voted 9-3 against approval of deramiocel for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) cardiomyopathy. Discussion on the primary upper limb function endpoint was more positive, and Capricor went back to the FDA in August with additional data and a refined indication focused on upper limb function. This pushed the FDA’s target action date from Aug. 22—a deadline that had already passed when Capricor announced the delay—to Nov. 22.
Capricor has also slowed programs not directly related to deramiocel, including the biotech’s exosome-based platform, in order to prioritize the DMD cell therapy “pending further regulatory clarity,” according to its third quarter earnings report on Tuesday.
This decision is unlikely to please Kaos Capital. The firm, which in an August letter to other company stakeholders described itself as a “significant and growing shareholder” of Capricor, urged a greater focus on the company’s efforts outside of deramiocel. Other Kaos demands included “an immediate meeting, board change, and capital-preservation plan.”

Capricor ramps up manufacturing spend ahead of FDA decision for DMD therapy

Capricor also revealed on Tuesday that it has initiated regulatory engagement in Europe and Japan for deramiocel. The company is also considering expanding the therapy into younger patients with DMD and Becker muscular dystrophy, a similar but less severe form of the disease, “with next steps to be informed by the U.S. regulatory outcome for Deramiocel,” according to the earnings report.
Capricor last month presented open label extension data from HOPE-3 showing that patients who transferred to the cell therapy after a year on placebo saw upper limb decline slow by 76% compared to their prior year data. These data were included in the August amendment. And on Monday, Capricor revealed that an abstract outlining the therapy’s cardiac results from HOPE-3 and presented at the American Heart Association (AHA) conference this month received AHA’s Outstanding Research Award in Pediatric Cardiology.
Compared to placebo, treatment with deramiocel slowed the progression of heart muscle scarring as measured by cardiac MRI, Capricor CEO Linda Marbán said on Tuesday’s earnings call. While the difference in ejection fraction across all patients did not reach statistical significance, in patients with existing cardiomyopathy this metric improved by approximately 2.8 percentage points relative to placebo, Marbán noted.
There are currently no therapies available specifically targeting cardiomyopathy, which is the leading cause of death for patients with DMD, Marbán told BioSpace in August last year.
“Put simply, the data tell a consistent story,” Marbán said on the call. “One year, two years, two randomized trials and a decade of clinical experience all points in the same direction. We do not believe that this is a case that rests solely on unmet medical need, secondary endpoints or regulatory flexibility.”

All of Navoiyuran's uranium operations in Uzbekistan use in-situ recovery mining. Credit: Navoiyuran
Posted By: Blair McBride November 11, 2026
Uzbekistan aims to double uranium production by 2030 to a level exceeding Canada’s entire 2024 output, as state-owned Navoiyuran develops new deposits and reduces its reliance on sulphuric acid.
The Central Asian country is targeting 15,000 tonnes a year, up from an expected 7,500 tonnes in 2026, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s office said Nov. 5. Canada produced about 14,300 tonnes in 2024, according to Natural Resources Canada.
“In particular, the share of reagents used as alternatives to sulfuric acid is expected to reach 40 percent by 2030,” the president’s office said.
The planned increase would add 7,500 tonnes a year to the nuclear fuel market. Delivering that growth will depend on developing deposits and securing processing chemicals, whose availability has also shaped production plans at neighbouring Kazakhstan’s Kazatomprom (LSE: KAP).
Production targets
The 2030 goal was announced in March, when the government also targeted 8,000 tonnes for 2026. November’s statement puts this year’s figure at 7,500 tonnes without explaining the difference. The Northern Miner has asked the President’s office for clarification.
State-owned Navoiyuran produced 7,000 tonnes of natural uranium in 2025, a 35% increase from 2024, the company said. That places it among the world’s six largest producers, according to UxC data published in the third quarter.
Kazatomprom, the world’s largest uranium producer, reported output of 25,839 tonnes in 2025 on a 100% basis, including its partners’ shares. Its own attributable production was 13,519 tonnes.
Like those of Kazatomprom, Navoiyuran’s uranium operations all use in-situ recovery (ISR), which injects a solution underground to dissolve uranium. The uranium-bearing solution is then pumped to the surface for processing. The technique generally requires less infrastructure than open-pit or underground mining.
Reducing acid use
Plans call for new production plants and infrastructure, additional sorption units and increased supplies of chemical reagents, including sulphur, Mirziyoyev’s office said.
Uzbekistan also aims to expand its explored uranium reserves to 200,000 tonnes by 2030, the president’s office said. Navoiyuran operates 43 deposits and separately reported ore reserves containing 96,600 tonnes of uranium under the JORC Code as of Jan. 1, 2026, without disclosing the proven and probable breakdown or average grade.
Kazatomprom has identified sulphuric acid availability as a condition of its 2026 production guidance.
Separately, equipment problems at the sulphuric acid plant at Orano’s McClean Lake mill forced Cameco (TSX: CCO; NYSE: CCJ) to temporarily suspend production at its Cigar Lake mine in Saskatchewan in July. The mine subsequently resumed production.
Navoiyuran’s net profit rose 138% to $348 million (C$491.5 million) in the first half of 2026, from $146.2 million in the same period of 2025, the company said Oct. 30.
Major new mine
Navoiyuran started commercial production at its Qizilkok mine in the country’s central Navoi region in April . The deposit contains 9,400 tonnes of uranium in preliminary JORC-compliant ore reserves as of Jan. 1, 2026, according to the company’s April 24 statement , which does not disclose the reserve grade or proven/probable breakdown. Qizilkok has a projected mine life of 15 years and annual production capacity of 1,200 tonnes.
Located about 400 km west of the capital Tashkent, Qizilkok is the company’s third-largest deposit by uranium reserves behind its core operations of Sugrali and Uchkuduk.
Navoiyuran became a standalone company in 2022, when it was spun out from the Soviet-era state conglomerate Navoi Mining and Metallurgical Combine.
The government’s April 2025 privatization plans included an initial public offering of a 10% to 15% stake in Navoiyuran, initially targeted for the second half of 2026. The government’s investment portal describes such timetables as indicativeand it hasn’t identified a listing exchange.
Uzbekistan also announced a $2.6-billion initiative last year to develop 76 projects covering 28 minerals over three years.

The U.S. Postal Service reported a $6.5 billion net loss for fiscal 2026, down from $9 billion a year earlier. Operating revenue rose 3% to $82.9 billion in the year ended Sept. 30, helped by growth in its Ground Advantage package service and higher postage rates.
What’s Related
Higher revenue and a $2.4 billion drop in workers’ compensation expense helped narrow the loss. USPS attributed much of that expense change to a reassessment of existing claims and changes in the rates used to estimate future costs. Its controllable loss, which excludes certain expenses outside management’s control, fell to $2.4 billion from $2.7 billion.
The Postal Service cut 19 million work hours and made changes to how it moves mail and packages by air and ground. Transportation expenses still rose by $225 million, driven in part by higher fuel costs. Compensation and benefits expenses rose by $456 million.
Package revenue rises as volume falls
Shipping and package revenue rose $1.7 billion, or 5.1%, to $34.1 billion. USPS handled 359 million fewer packages than the year before, a 5.3% drop. A temporary price increase that took effect in April helped lift revenue.
Ground Advantage was a bright spot. Revenue from the service rose 17.1% to about $19.6 billion, and volume grew 10.5% to nearly 3.3 billion packages. Ground Advantage offers delivery in two to five days for packages weighing up to 70 pounds.
First-Class Mail and Marketing Mail also brought in more revenue even as both handled fewer pieces. For parcel shippers , a separate round of holiday price increases took effect Oct. 4 and is scheduled to end Jan. 17.
USPS asks Congress to raise borrowing limit
The Postal Service is asking Congress to raise its $15 billion borrowing limit, which has been in place since 1992. It is also seeking changes to how pension costs are divided between USPS and the Treasury, along with more flexibility to invest pension and retiree health funds.
“Because of our ongoing financial crisis, we are continuing to balance the needs of our daily business operations with our need to conserve cash,” Postmaster General David Steiner said. USPS deferred about $2.6 billion in federal retirement contributions during the fiscal year, payments it will eventually have to make.
Earlier this year, USPS warned it could run out of cash as soon as 2027. In June, Steiner told lawmakers that revised projections put a potential cash shortfall between 2031 and 2034. The agency continues to ask Congress to change or help pay for some of the requirements that add to its costs.

Nearly half of supply chain and planning professionals say their technology is more ready for AI than their rules for overseeing it. Forty-eight percent rated their technology platforms higher than their AI governance, which covers decisions such as when a tool can act on its own and when someone needs to sign off, according to a new survey by RELEX Solutions.
What’s Related
“Technology isn’t the primary limitation to becoming an AI-ready company,” RELEX said in the report.
Governance had the lowest average score of the five areas RELEX looked at, at 4.4 out of 10. It ranked last or tied for last for 58% of respondents. Yet just 15% mentioned governance, risk, or security when describing their AI goals.
Laurence Brenig-Jones, vice president of product at RELEX, gave an example: “When AI recommends buying more inventory, acting on that recommendation commits cash.” He said finance, planning, and operations teams should agree up front on what the system can do, which decisions need approval, and what results would justify giving it more authority.
The data comes from the RELEX State of Supply Chain AI Practitioner Pulse, based on intake surveys from 108 registrants at 80 organizations across retail , manufacturing , consumer packaged goods , and distribution. They came from five groups in the company’s 2026 AI Masterclass Series and rated their companies on a 10-point scale. RELEX said the sample was self-selected and the results “are not representative of the industries as a whole.”
Most companies gave themselves poor scores
Overall AI readiness averaged 4.9 out of 10, and only 8% of respondents rated their organizations 7 or higher. Planning processes and change leadership tied for the highest average at 5.1, while data and technology platforms each averaged 4.9.
When asked about their AI goals, 32% mentioned finding practical uses or figuring out where to start, and 30% mentioned building a strategy or roadmap. One in five brought up measuring return on investment . RELEX counted more than one theme in an answer when it applied.
Retail leads, governance comes last
Retail respondents averaged 5.3 for overall readiness, compared with 4.5 for manufacturing and CPG. The widest gaps were in planning processes (5.8 vs. 4.6) and technology platforms (5.4 vs. 4.3). Governance came last for both groups, at 4.7 for retail and 4.1 for manufacturing and CPG.
RELEX recommended starting with decisions that are made often, tie directly to a measurable financial impact, and have enough data to track progress. The company also suggested reviewing AI performance, exceptions, and manual overrides weekly, then giving the tool more room to act as trust and results improve.

Facelifted 2028 Mercedes SL Roadster To Gain Benz Line
20 photos
Photo: Mercedes-AMG
The Mercedes-Benz SL will return in 2027, joining the facelifted AMG and Maybach lines. Giving the canvas-topped roadster a third personality makes plenty of sense. Rather than chasing aggressive performance or extravagant luxury, the Benz would put greater emphasis on relaxed open-top motoring.
None other than chief executive officer Ola Kallenius provided the confirmation, and he did so during the Golden Steering Wheel awards ceremony in Berlin. Speaking to Auto Bild, the big kahuna also posed for a photograph that included a camouflaged example of the 2028 Mercedes-Benz SL.
The German automaker's three-pointed star dominates the front grille, and this badge is flanked by star-motif running lights in the headlights. A cleaner front bumper design hides under the camo wrap, giving the Benz a distinct visual identity from the Panamericana-grilled AMG or the ultra-lux Maybach with its monolithic grille design and look-at-me wheel choices.
Kallenius explained that Merc is giving each SL version a distinct purpose, with the Benz combining improved comfort with the roof down, a more balanced relationship between sporting ability and refinement, and timeless styling. With the 2028 model year, the SL is also expected to drop the poor-selling turbo inline-four engine that currently powers the AMG SL 43.
The 43 also happens to be Mercedes-AMG's only rear-drive SL as of this writing. At the end of the day, Formula 1 powertrain technologies don't matter too much when you're getting a puny 2.0-liter mill for a simply ridiculous 126,686.45 euros. That kind of money can get you much nicer or more performance-oriented vehicles, for sure!
Photo: Mercedes-AMG Opting for the 55 results in the M177 twin-turbo V8, whereas the 63 offers a bit more oomph from said 4.0-liter unit. And finally, the 63 with plug-in hybrid assistance offers a tremendous 805 horsepower and 1,047 pound-feet (1,420 Newton-meters) of twist.
Unfortunately, the plug-in part of the powertrain was not designed with electric range in mind. That's why the SL 63 S E PERFORMANCE can't do better than 13 kilometers in the WLTP, a figure that can be alternatively interpreted as 8 miles. The Maybach line is only available in 680 specification, which uses the aforementioned cross-plane V8.
This lump develops a respectable 585 ps (577 hp) and 800 Nm (590 lb-ft) between 2,500 and 5,000 rpm. Come 2027, all V8 options are likely to be replaced by the M177 Evo flat-plane V8. The switch from a cross- to a flat-plane crankshaft results in a different soundtrack, but Mercedes and the AMG division also decided on it due to emission regulations.
While a CPC fires two cylinders consecutively on the same bank, the FPC alternates firing evenly between the left and right cylinder banks of a V-type engine, thus creating the more exotic sounds we associate with flat-plane mills. The alternating exhaust pulses happen to eliminate exhaust gas interference between cylinders, allowing the hot-V turbos to spool more cleanly.
Speaking of cleanly, the M177 Evo runs the Miller cycle to maintain a stoichiometric air-fuel ratio under high load. While a V8 engine is plausible for the Benz SL, an I6 would suit its character much better. After all, the original 300 SL from the 1950s came with a straight-six mill. The 3.0-liter engine of the CLE 53 is a great candidate, with AMG claiming 443 horsepower and either 413 or 443 pound-feet (560 or 600 Newton-meters) with overboost active.

Can you believe it’s been more than two decades since Lamborghini unveiled the Gallardo ? Why, of course you can, as even though it may still be a stunning machine even by today’s standards, it was eventually replaced by the Huracan, which made way for the Temerario.
The Huracan was assembled from 2014 to 2024, and the Temerario, which is the Raging Bull’s new-age “baby” supercar, featuring a 4.0-liter twin-turbo plug-in hybrid V8, with 907 hp (920 ps/677 kW) combined, and 0-62 mph (0-100 kph) in 2.7 seconds, entered production at Sant’Agata Bolognese, Italy, in 2025.
Production of the Lamborghini Gallardo spanned from 2003 to 2013, and it is estimated that a little over 14,000 units were put together during this time. The lineup was vast, as it included the original Gallardo Coupe and Spyder, as well as the Superleggera, and the LP 560-4 Coupe and Spyder, LP 570-4 Superleggera, LP 570-4 Spyder Performante, LP 550-2 Coupe and Spyder, and others, which were part of the facelift that came out at the Geneva Motor Show back in 2008.
Pictured in the gallery is a 2009 Lamborghini Gallardo LP 560-4 Coupe, featuring an orange exterior and an orange and black interior. It’s registered in Calgary, AB, Canada, and it has a dealer behind it that reportedly bought it in September 2026, adding some 100 miles (~160 km) since. The vendor tried to part ways with it on Cars&Bids, yet when the online auction ended on November 10, 2026, the reserve was not met, so the supercar failed to change hands.
Photo: Cars&Bids More on that in a few moments, as first, we have to delve into some of its aspects, including the equipment. This Gallardo features 19-inch wheels, has green brake calipers, a transparent engine cover, and a nose-lift system to clear speed bumps and steep driveways easier. The dual-zone automatic climate control system and the leather upholstery are also mentioned in the ad.
There are also a few modifications on deck, such as the front and rear bumpers, as well as the floor mats and carpet covers. The chips and clearcoat cracks on the apron and rear diffuser, a pitting on the windshield, a chip on the roof panel, and a taillight bulb that needs to be replaced are some of the known flaws. This Lamborghini Gallardo also has wear on the driver’s seat and some interior plastic trim.
Moreover, the selling dealer also noted that the vehicle will lock/unlock automatically when the key fob is in proximity, and that the head unit display does not move anymore, so the access to the CD player is restricted. Thus, its next owner will have some things to sort out if they want their modern-classic supercar to return to its original shine.
Power is supplied by a V10 engine, as every petrolhead and their pet can tell you. The naturally aspirated mill has a 5.2-liter displacement, and in this case, it pumps out 552 hp (560 ps/412 kW) and 398 pound-feet (540 Nm) of torque. The engine drives all four wheels through a six-speed automated manual transmission. The 0-62 mph (0-100 kph) took 3.7 seconds when the car was new, and the top speed was 202 mph (325 kph).
Photo: Cars&Bids The listing shows that the supercar is accompanied by one key and that’s it, and that it is not eligible for import into the United States of America, and this is likely why it hasn’t got a lot of attention from bidders. After all, these things tend to fetch from $130,000 to $175,000 in our market these days, and cars with less than 20,000 miles (32,000 km) are considered low-mileage examples. This one checks this box, as it had 18,000 miles (29,000 km) on the odometer at the time of cataloging.
It is worth noting that this 2009 Lamborghini Gallardo LP 560-4 Coupe is still searching for a new home as we speak, after failing to change hands. The supercar was advertised on Cars&Bids as part of an online auction that recently ended (November 10, 2026), and it will be interesting to find out how much the vendor hopes to get from it. The highest bid was $68,000, and the reserve was not met.
So, if you are searching for a modern-classic “baby” supercar from Lamborghini that is considered a low-mileage example, albeit one that needs some work, with emphasis on the fact that you cannot import it to the States, then this one might just be the right machine for you. But assuming you were actually shopping for a cool Lamborghini Gallardo north of the US border and you came across this one, how much would you have paid for it?

A truck is seen at a Barrick mine in Nevada. Credit: Barrick Mining via Facebook.
Posted By: FREDERIC TOMESCO November 11, 2026
Barrick Mining (TSX: ABX; NYSE: B) has filed to take its North American gold business public in New York, advancing a planned share sale that could return cash to investors while leaving the parent in control.
The new company, American Barrick Gold, expects to pay an annual base dividend of $1.25 billion (C$1.77 billion), distributed quarterly to its shareholders, the company disclosed Tuesday . Payments would remain subject to board approval and financial conditions.
Barrick’s filing “highlights American Barrick Gold as a pure-play gold producer with low geopolitical risk, producing about 2 million oz. at about $1,800 per oz. of all-in sustaining costs with a 20-year reserve life,” Scotia Capital mining analyst Tanya Jakusconec said in a note published late Tuesday. The filing gives investors a clearer view of the assets behind Barrick’s proposed separation. Barrick’s Fourmile mine in Nevada offers future growth, but the larger development scenario carries a much higher construction bill and relies heavily on inferred resources.
Joint venture
The new company would hold Barrick’s 61.5% interest in the Nevada Gold Mines joint venture and 60% of the Pueblo Viejo mine in the Dominican Republic. Newmont (NYSE, ASX: NEM) is the partner in both operations.
Nevada Gold Mines accounted for 81% of Barrick’s 2025 attributable production. American Barrick will be based in Henderson, Nevada. The filing follows an August agreement to contribute Barrick’s Fourmile project and Newmont’s Mike and Fiberline properties to Nevada Gold Mines. Newmont agreed to pay Barrick $1.95 billion while leaving their joint venture ownership split unchanged. The agreement also secured Newmont’s consent to the listing, Barrick said Monday.
“Today’s filing provides greater visibility into Nevada Gold Mines’ growth outlook and Fourmile’s development potential,” National Bank Financial mining analyst Shane Nagle said in a note.
Costs climb
Fourmile’s preliminary capital estimate has risen to about $2.6 billion from $1.5 billion–$1.7 billion in the 2025 assessment, according to the filing. The larger scenario envisages annual output of 750,000–850,000 oz. at full production in 2034, versus 600,000–750,000 oz. previously. Estimated all-in sustaining costs rose to $850–$950 per ounce from $650–$750. Those figures use gold prices of $3,568 and $2,585 per oz., respectively, BMO Capital Markets mining analyst Matthew Murphy said in a note late Tuesday. About 83% of the resources in the larger economic scenario are inferred, a category too uncertain to support mineral reserves. The assessment remains preliminary and doesn’t represent a construction commitment, American Barrick said. Using its long-term gold price of $4,000 per oz., BMO calculates Fourmile’s net asset value at $13.5 billion on a 100% basis, above the $10 billion it carries in its model. Excluding inferred resources reduces that sensitivity value to about $1.6 billion, Murphy said.
Proceeds and control
American Barrick plans to seek a New York Stock Exchange listing under ABGC, with Barrick retaining majority ownership. The number of shares and offering price have yet to be set, and the registration statement hasn’t become effective, Barrick said.
Part of the proceeds would repay a note issued to Toronto-based parent Barrick, with the remainder for general corporate purposes. While Barrick expects to return the proceeds it receives to its shareholders, it hasn’t specified the size or form of those returns.
American Barrick also aims to pay special dividends from excess free cash flow after reinvestment and growth spending. Its framework targets $1 billion of net cash, with $2 billion of flexibility either side. Payouts remain at the board’s discretion.
2026 goal
CEO Mark Hill, who will lead American Barrick, said Monday that the offering could close this year or in early 2027, depending on the securities regulator’s review. “We’re still trying to get this done this year but it may slide into January,” Hill told analysts on the conference call.
Goldman Sachs, Bank of America Securities, Citigroup and RBC Capital Markets will lead the IPO, according to the filing.
Barrick shares fell 0.4% to C$56.21 Wednesday morning in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$92 billion ($66 billion). The stock has traded between C$45.28 and C$74 over the past year.

Photo: Bring a Trailer
There's a very interesting story behind this particular ZR1X, and there's nothing collectors love more than buying a car with an interesting story behind it. Actually, I think everyone would enjoy that. It's the equivalent of George Costanza buying an '89 LeBaron just because he thought it was once owned by Jon Voight.
By the way, George was duped in more ways than one regarding that car, and so were we. It was presented on the show as an '89 LeBaron, when in reality it was a 1984 Chrysler LeBaron Town & Country Convertible according to the IMCDB. His car belonged to the earlier K-car based LeBaron generation. So yeah, Georgie boy was deceived.
Where am I going with this? Well, like I said, there's an interesting story behind this 2026 ZR1X as well. The car was used by General Motors as a pre-production evaluation vehicle, also known as a Captured Test Fleet (CTF) vehicle - part of their internal testing and evaluation program. To clarify, this wasn't some experimental/engineering prototype or even a regular pre-production vehicle.
The latter would often come with provisional components in order to mirror a final spec. A "close but no cigar" type of thing. Whereas a CTF vehicle is basically a near-production car driven by GM personnel to identify any issues before customer deliveries can commence. This Vette was "tested" for only 302 miles before ending up with a Minneapolis-based dealer, who then decided to auction it off to the highest bidder.
According to the sticker, this would have retailed for $247,855, and the price for which it just sold is an impressive $355,000 (plus a buyer's fee). While that might sound like a lot (and it is), I believe this is now one of the cheapest ZR1X models sold at auction in recent months. The absolute cheapest one was a Red Mist Metallic example with 1,200 miles on the clock that exchanged hands for $315,000 last month.
In terms of specs, this car is finished in black and comes with a carbon-fiber rear wing, hood spoiler, and dive planes - all courtesy of the Carbon Fiber Aero Package. Additionally, it also features a carbon fiber rear split window, LED headlights, front and rear cameras, plus a set of Carbon Flash 20" and 21" forged wheels rocking Michelin tires and carbon-ceramic discs.
Photo: Bring a Trailer Meanwhile, interior highlights include the Sky Cool Gray leather GT2 bucket seats, carbon fiber trim accents, a performance data and video recorder, dual-zone automatic climate control, cruise control, a 14-speaker Bose Performance Series sound system, a head-up display, and loads more. This thing is loaded.
As for the engine, you already know what you're rocking with. It's a twin-turbocharged 5.5-liter LT7 V8 working alongside an electric motor and a 1.9-kWh liquid-cooled lithium-ion battery pack. Together, they combine for 1,250 horsepower and 973 lb-ft of torque, sending everything to all four wheels via an eight-speed dual-clutch automatic.

U.S. service members attend a briefing and material demonstration by ICScape, a cybersecurity escape room by the Idaho National Laboratory at the Professional Education Center in Little Rock, Ark., July 22, 2026. (Texas National Guard photo by Spc. Paul Zepeda.)
Enterprise Super Intelligence (SI), a powerful tool for sorting through and evaluating data to help enable faster, better-informed decision-making, is only as good as the data it is fed. Protecting against attempts to compromise security or inject malicious data is paramount to ensuring that autonomous systems can be trusted to give accurate, timely evaluations of the data they are analyzing.
“Trust isn’t an abstract, ethical debate; it’s a non-negotiable operational requirement,” said Mandy Satterwhite, Managing Director and Cyber Lead at Accenture Federal Services. “In the heat of battle, if an autonomous system relies on poisoned data, yields an unexplainable result, or silently fails behind the scenes, it doesn’t give you an advantage; it creates unacceptable operational risk.”
Ensuring SI tools can be trusted requires a comprehensive security strategy, rigorous data governance, and an operational balance between protection and accessibility.
Autonomous systems are useless without trust
SI enables decision-making on the battlefield by quickly sorting through massive volumes of data and providing the information needed to give commanders a clearer picture of the situation. If a commander is looking at satellite images of a target and has system-generated data on what has changed, such as an unexpected concentration of armored assets at a contested perimeter, that intelligence informs immediate tactical maneuvers. But if that feed has been poisoned or spoofed, commanders may make wrong decisions because their situational awareness isn’t accurate.
“When command and control (C2) systems synthesize options for a decision-maker, that leader must know with absolute certainty that those recommendations are built on authoritative, untampered data under our control,” said Satterwhite. “If you can’t trace data provenance or explain how the conclusion was derived, you can’t act on it in combat because mission success is on the line.”
Service members from Paraguay and Kenya participate in a cybersecurity exercise as part of Cyber Shield 2026 at the Professional Education Center in Little Rock, Ark., July 13, 2026. (Texas Army National Guard photo by Staff Sgt. Jason Archer.)
In many ways this is a supply chain problem, especially when commercial models are being adopted for military use. When defense components adapt commercial frontier models for tactical mission systems, they inherit the training data and dependencies of that foundation. If that upstream pipeline is compromised, the vulnerability transfers directly to the battlefield.
Another challenge is using the right model for the job. While large-scale frontier models are powerful in many use cases, they may not be ideal for the specialized capabilities the US military needs. The models must be sized properly and their foundational elements, such as data sources and model weights, must be audited to verify their architectural integrity and fitness for high-consequence environments, said Satterwhite.
“We’ve seen adversaries attempt to manipulate model weight files directly to skew outputs. If you don’t control and verify the digital supply chain from end to end, you are building on shaky ground.”
Cybersecurity concerns
SI is a double-edged sword for information management. While it can sort through massive datasets at speeds unimaginable for humans, it can also power cyberattacks that can overwhelm security protocols and compromise data.
Traditional cybersecurity compliance methods, such as periodic penetration tests or pre-deployment checklists, cannot identify cyberattacks and enable responses quickly enough to keep pace with autonomous, machine-speed threat landscapes. When adversaries can use automated tools to constantly probe for vulnerabilities, then strike instantly when one is identified, periodic testing of security is insufficient.
“Advanced frontier models have completely collapsed the cyberattack timeline,” said Satterwhite. “Cyber defense has to move to continuous, automated validation, similar to the concept of ‘fighting fire with fire.’”
Establishing that defensive posture requires integrating automated red-teaming and continuous vulnerability validation directly into software pipelines. By doing so, code, models, and agentic workflows can be continuously tested against real-world attack scenarios, allowing for simultaneous validation of security protocols to ensure data can be protected.
Traditionally, adding layers of cybersecurity has been viewed with suspicion, as it is seen as slowing down operations. Implementing security protocols from the start can overcome that potential slowdown, said Satterwhite.
“The idea that security and speed are mutually exclusive is the biggest misconception in the industry,” she said. “When security is treated as an afterthought or a final inspection at the end of a multi-year development cycle, yes, it halts progress and causes massive delays. But when you bake security directly into the architecture from day one, security becomes an accelerator.”
Balancing security and accessibility
While cybersecurity is important to protect against intrusions or data adulteration, it must be balanced with allowing access for those who need it. If warfighters in the field must constantly navigate cumbersome security barriers or face data lockouts under fire, operational readiness breaks down.
The key to striking that balance is engineering advanced systems as an augmentation capability with human-in-the-loop validation, rather than an unguided autonomous system. While digital tools can process and evaluate data, humans must be in ultimate control of decision-making and access. By building architectures that allow for human operators to take full advantage of the speed and powerful data collection, collation, and management SI can offer, operators can fully maximize these capabilities while working with trusted, reliable data.
“In sensitive warfighting environments, keeping a human decision-maker in the lead is paramount,” said Satterwhite. “That means engineering explicit architectural guardrails, OODA-loop feedback checkpoints, and hard kill switches directly into the system architecture. An autonomous model can rapidly process unstructured sensor data and surface three actionable courses of action, for example, but a human operator must evaluate those verified choices at a deliberate checkpoint before execution. That structure buys down risk, protects mission integrity, and ensures command authority remains exactly where it belongs.”

DHL Supply Chain is testing warehouse robots that can decide how to respond when conditions change. The company is also rolling out AI software in live warehouses to help site managers coordinate workers, robots, and other equipment as orders come in.
What’s Related
DHL announced the moves earlier this week. The software is moving into day-to-day use after an initial test, while the adaptive robots are still in pilot programs.
“Our immediate priority is to continue scaling our proven robotics across more sites while moving the next generation of adaptive AI-powered robotics from pilots into live operations,” said Tim Tetzlaff, DHL Supply Chain’s global head of digital transformation.
DHL says conventional warehouse robots typically follow set routes or instructions. The robots it’s testing are given a task to complete and can use information about their surroundings to decide how to proceed if conditions differ from what they expected. The company did not specify which jobs the adaptive robots are being tested on or report how they performed in the pilots.
RELATED STORIES: Six Trends Changing How Robots Work in Warehouses | Before You Buy Warehouse Robots, Know What You’re Trying to Fix
How it comes together
DHL calls the software AI orchestration. It acts as a control center, pulling together data from warehouse systems so site managers can adjust how they use workers and equipment as demand changes.
In one workflow DHL is testing, the software connects mobile robots and automated packing equipment with the warehouse management system , which tracks orders and directs work. DHL says the setup uses incoming order data to shift resources, which can help warehouses process more orders. It did not say how much more.
Robots at scale
DHL says it has deployed more than 9,000 robots worldwide. Its robots have made more than 1.5 billion picks , and Boston Dynamics’ Stretch robots have unloaded 10 million cases at DHL sites.
The company has used advanced analytics and AI tools more than 1,400 times, including more than 500 deployments in 2026. It also logged more than 2.5 million minutes of interactions with conversational AI tools. DHL says more than 95% of its warehouses worldwide already use advanced digital tools.
Where warehouse workers fit in
DHL says robots can handle repetitive, physically demanding work, while employees use their judgment to handle situations that fall outside the usual routine.
“The most successful supply chains will not be fully automated,” Tetzlaff said. “They will combine the speed and analytical capabilities of technology with the experience and judgment of people.”

Less than two weeks away from a highly anticipated FDA ruling on its cell therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Capricor Therapeutics has reported increased investment in its San Diego plant to support commercial production.
Capricor Therapeutics’ operating expenses jumped 70% in the third quarter as the company scaled up manufacturing and otherwise prepared to market its Duchenne muscular dystrophy cell therapy, which the FDA is set to decide on by Nov. 22.
Preparing for launch, Capricor spent $44.7 million in the third quarter, compared with $26.3 million one year ago. The biotech cited precommercial activities and manufacturing scale-up as the primary drivers of increased spending.
Capricor’s facility in San Diego is “up and running and ready to supply an initial launch if deramiocel is approved,” CEO Linda Marbán said on the biotech’s third-quarter earnings call Tuesday. The company will support the initial launch from a first-floor cleanroom, which has undergone a pre-license inspection and can make enough doses for 250 patients per year, the CEO said.
The biotech is adding manufacturing capacity on the second floor of the facility to increase output. Once Capricor completes the expansion, the facility will have the capacity to support about 2,000 to 2,500 patients a year, Marbán said.
Capricor’s second-floor production plant “is pretty much built out” and scheduled to undergo validation during the first half of next year, the CEO added. Capricor will finish cleanrooms on the second floor “in sequential order as demand implies,” she said. The cleanrooms are part of a long-term plan to meet demand for deramiocel.
“We don’t anticipate that supply will be a problem, either in early stages of launch or as we continue commercial development,” Marbán said. “If we are lucky enough to get approval in the U.S., we’re poised to continue the expansion of our manufacturing footprint into a new facility in San Diego, which we’ve already tentatively agreed to occupy and build out should the need prevail.”
Manufacturing issues contributed to the rejection of Capricor’s first filing for approval in 2025, as the FDA’s complete response letter cited certain deficiencies regarding deramiocel’s chemistry, manufacturing, and controls (CMC).
With an advisory committee recently voting 9-3 against approval of the cell therapy, the biotech faces doubts about whether it will bring deramiocel to market on its second attempt. Capricor is “focusing primarily on approval” but has spoken internally about what additional work it could do if the FDA rejects its filing, Marbán said.
In response to a question regarding investment in another possible clinical trial, Marbán said she would be “reluctant to say goodbye to deramiocel if it required some simple clinical work that could further support it.”
If the FDA rejects deramiocel, the CEO said Capricor will assess the feedback and act “prudently based on if we think that there’s a way to establish greater efficacy and/or safety doing another clinical trial.”

The Newest Mobi XL Tiny House Adds an Extra Room to a Luxurious Layout
46 photos
Photo: Mobi House
How to make an XL tiny house even better – that is something where Mobi House excels. This highly reputable European builder with one of the most prolific portfolios on the market is an expert in modern Scandinavian-style tiny homes, from the ultra-compact ones to luxurious XL designs. Its latest model, the Mobi Kolos Island, takes things to a new level.
When you say XL tiny house, you immediately think of a supremely spacious layout that doesn’t sacrifice any of the common living spaces of a conventional house. With Mobi Kolos Island, the newest addition to its Mobile Line series, Mobi House enhances flexibility by adding an extra room that can become many things, depending on each owner’s preferences and needs.
Mobile Line is the Polish builder’s premium home series, comprised of 10-meter-long (32.8 feet) models with full-size bedrooms, kitchens, lounges, and bathrooms. Ideal for families but just as great for couples and individual owners who simply want the comfort of uncompromising spaciousness, the XL tiny homes in this series are all about luxury.
Photo: Mobi House After the success of Mobi Kolos Mountains, Mobi Kolos Sea, and Mobi Kolos Desert, the Polish builder is truly breaking the norm with a new model that is more impressive than anything before it. Mobi Kolos Island is really a mini mansion on wheels, extremely versatile , and beautifully furnished in the best Scandinavian style.
A proven two-bedroom layout with a ground-floor bedroom and a loft is made even more versatile by adding an extra room defined as a multi-purpose space. Smaller than the ground-floor two-person bedroom, this compact room can be turned into a second ground-floor bedroom for one, a kids’ room with bunk beds, a lovely, private home office, or even a spacious walk-in wardrobe (just the idea of a tiny house with a separate walk-in wardrobe is pure luxury).
A generous 3-meter (9.8 feet) width, together with the XL length, leads to a spacious layout offering more than 26 square meters (280 square feet) of floor space. As a result, future owners will be able to enjoy a perfect kitchen, a lounge/dining area that’s big enough for the entire family, a stylish bathroom, and multiple bedrooms that can comfortably accommodate up to six people.
Photo: Mobi House The wagon-like configuration includes a wide corridor from one end of the house to another, while all the living and service areas spill effortlessly from one another. This type of design is highly space-efficient and also modern, with the corridor adding just the right level of separation, as well as seamless access from one end of the home to the other. Large windows throughout keep the entire home filled with natural light, making it seem even bigger.
A modern configuration like this strikes the perfect balance between privacy and openness. In a tiny house, personal space can sometimes be challenging, just as much as bringing people together around the dining table. This new XL tiny house takes care of both issues. With the main bedroom and the extra multi-purpose room, it adds two enclosed spaces for full privacy, while the lounge is big enough to welcome all six people.
The lounge itself is a flexible space. Owners can choose to use it as a classic living room. In that case, it would be furnished with a typical Mobi custom sofa bench, an L-shaped design with built-in storage and comfy cushioning. A large TV mounted on the wall and a classic coffee table complete the setup. If they choose to turn this into a dining room, there’s enough space for an ingenious foldable oak table, with bench seats on one side, and regular chairs on the other side.
Photo: Mobi House This gorgeous dining room version, inspired by diner booths, is one of the most spacious and comfortable you’ll ever see in a tiny house. It doesn’t just make room for the whole family, but it offers the best view on both sides – those seated on the bench are facing the main entry, which is entirely glazed, while those seated on the chairs are facing the two large, horizontal windows in the lounge, separate by a custom shelf for storage and decorative display.
Nestled between the kitchen and the bedroom exterior wall, this versatile lounge/dining room feels a lot cozier, too. Plus, that exterior wall (cleverly turned into a feature wall for a style boost) acts as the perfect canvas for additional décor, which makes this relaxation nook even more elegant.
The kitchen is also U-shaped, with an L-shaped countertop on one side, and a full cabinetry wall on the other side. This is the kind of tiny house kitchen where nobody will miss the storage capacity of a conventional kitchen. Lower cupboards, floating shelves, and a full cabinetry wall offer monster storage that will keep everything perfectly organized.
Photo: Mobi House High-quality appliances are also impeccably incorporated, including a dishwasher and a washer/dryer that wouldn’t fit in the bathroom. The furniture is custom-made, so owners can choose between laminated plywood, oak, or composite, depending on their budget and style preferences. Expensive finishes can take this XL tiny house to a truly luxurious level, comparable to a mini-mansion.
The main bedroom also features a lot of built-in cabinets and generous closet space beyond what you could typically expect in a tiny house. Posted By: FREDERIC TOMESCO November 11, 2026
Altius Minerals (TSX: ALS) agreed to buy TNR Gold (TSXV: TNR) in a deal valued at $122 million (US$86 million) that boosts the company’s exposure to Argentine copper and lithium while spinning out an Alaska gold project.
Each eligible TNR share would receive 0.0072 Altius shares and a quarter-share in a new company holding the Shotgun gold project, Altius said Wednesday in a statement . The package’s estimated value of 48¢ includes 38¢ in Altius stock and 10¢ assigned to the spinout, representing a 60% premium to TNR’s 30¢ close Tuesday.
The acquisition fits Altius’s strategy of accumulating royalties on long-life mineral deposits. It combines potential future copper revenue from TNR’s royalty on McEwen Copper’s Los Azules project with exposure to Mariana, an operating lithium brine project where Altius already holds a royalty. TNR’s interests also include a royalty on properties within the Josemaria copper-gold project.
Los Azules “represents the primary long-term opportunity, while Mariana offers nearer-term cash flow potential,” TD Securities mining analyst Craig Hutchison said in a note.
Development timelines
Hutchison expects limited near-term financial impact from the relatively small deal, with its value dependent on development timelines at Los Azules and Josemaria.
The companies’ relationship deepened in May, when Altius completed a $4.2-million investment for a minority stake and secured first-offer rights over TNR’s principal royalties. By October, Altius owned about 13% of TNR, which disclosed an unsolicited takeover proposal and entered exclusive talks. TNR’s effective interests include a 0.36% net smelter return royalty on Los Azules and 1.35% on Mariana, excluding portions held for another shareholder.
McEwen project
Los Azules, in San Juan province, is owned by McEwen Copper , whose investors include McEwen (TSX: MUX; NYSE: MUX), Rio Tinto (ASX: RIO; LSE: RIO; NYSE: RIO) and automaker Stellantis. A 2025 feasibility study for the project outlines average annual production of about 148,200 tonnes of copper cathode over 21 years, with cash costs of US$1.71 per lb. The proposed operation would produce finished copper using heap leaching and solvent extraction-electrowinning, avoiding a conventional concentrator and reliance on outside smelters. Nearby exploration targets could eventually help extend the project’s operating life. Los Azules “offers the potential for decades of increased copper exposure within our portfolio,” Altius CEO Brian Dalton said Wednesday. McEwen Copper secured a US$240-million loan in August for engineering and early works. Full project financing and a final investment decision are targeted for mid-2027, with commercial production starting in 2030, subject to financing and approvals. That leaves the royalty’s copper cash flow dependent on successful development.
Buyback option
At Mariana, Ganfeng Lithium inaugurated a 20,000-tonne-per-year lithium chloride plant in February 2025. The acquisition would consolidate Altius’s exposure to the operation, although TNR’s royalty carries a buyback provision: Ganfeng’s subsidiary can purchase 0.9 percentage points of TNR’s effective interest for $900,000, reducing it to 0.45%. Shotgun would remain with former TNR shareholders through the spinout. Altius would retain a 0.5% royalty and invest $2.2 million to increase its spinout ownership to just under 20%, while providing technical support. Closing of the TNR acquisition is expected around the first quarter of 2027, subject to shareholder, court and regulatory approvals. Shareholders controlling about 28% of TNR have signed support agreements; a vote is expected in December. TNR shares closed Tuesday at 30¢ in Toronto, valuing the company at $73 million, before trading was halted Wednesday morning pending news. Altius was 3.5% weaker at $51.14 Wednesday, valuing it at $3 billion.

Unplugged Performance Wants To Continue Work on the Cybertruck, Should Tesla Give It the Green Light
66 photos
Photo: Tesla
Unplugged Performance, well-known for its Tesla performance parts, has offered to take the Cybertruck production line off Tesla's hands and continue to build the trucks while paying Tesla a license fee. If successful, this initiative will allow UP to expand the Cybertruck platform with an SUV and a cargo hauler. UP says it will fund production with a consortium of investors, allowing Tesla to focus on the Cybercab.
When Elon Musk announced the demise of the Cybertruck, he said that Tesla needs factory space at Giga Texas to increase Cybercab production. The explanation did not convince many people, especially as Giga Texas has plenty of room for expansion. Besides that, Tesla had to admit that it currently can't even run the Cybercab line continuously, because it has no use for the vehicles it produces.
In a later tweet, Musk offered another explanation: that Tesla doesn't have enough talented people. Maintaining the Cybertruck while at the same time ramping up the Cybercab production would spread them too thin. This is more accurate, considering how many talented engineers have left Tesla over the past two years.
Even though highly anticipated, considering the low sales numbers, the Cybertruck's demise signals a more disturbing trend: that Tesla is winding down its automotive operations, and the Cybertruck won't be the last to fall. As Tesla focuses on robots and robotaxis, perhaps its automotive business might be better off if offloaded to another company.
That's exactly what Unplugged Performance (UP) has proposed to Tesla, offering to buy the Cybertruck production line when it will be dismantled from Giga Texas next year. UP said that it's ready to line up a "consortium of investors" to run the line at no cost for Tesla.
This would be a win-win situation for everyone involved. Tesla gets to focus on Cybercab development and production, while freeing the company's resources, including floor space and headcount. Tesla also gains from license fees, plus FSD subscriptions and other revenue on every vehicle built.
Unplugged Performance will also get important benefits. The upfitter has a wide range of Cybertruck parts and upgrades, while also upfitting the Cybertruck for use by police departments in the US. The Cybertruck's disappearance would leave it with a significantly diminished business.
The initiative has already gathered impressive support, not least from former Tesla engineers who reached out offering to help. Unplugged Performance admitted that the Cybertruck might end up more expensive , while peak output might be lower until the new owner gets up to speed. Unplugged Performance bets not only on the Cybertruck, but also on a three-row CyberSUV and a CyberCargo hauler to vastly expand production and make the Cybertruck platform profitable.
A three-row SUV built on the Cybertruck's platform has been one of the most requested vehicles from Tesla fans. There's no reason to believe that it would not sell like hotcakes. Unplugged Performance also bets that vehicles built on the Cybertruck's platform could provide unique capabilities to Tesla's Robotaxi network, especially in situations where an off-road vehicle is required.
Despite the excitement surrounding this initiative, I doubt that Tesla would agree to such a move. If, God forbid, Unplugged Performance proves the Cybertruck platform is successful and profitable, Elon Musk risks being exposed as an incompetent CEO . On the other hand, I'm sure Musk must have considered spinning off the automotive business, especially as Tesla's Chinese operations might be an obstacle to the upcoming SpaceX merger. A fair question we’re hearing: can UP really run the Cybertruck vehicle line? Not alone, and not overnight. Tesla expects to dismantle the line around mid-2027. Until then, we’re organizing interested investors, recruiting experienced manufacturing talent and partners, and choosing a location. We’d like to be near Giga Texas. Production would need to ramp back up, and it may be cell constrained. Peak output may be lower and unit costs may be higher. A reset is hard, premature death is harder. We choose reset. We believe this is highly fundable because one production platform serves three markets: existing demand for the pickup, pent-up demand for a seven-seat SUV, and Robotaxi network vehicles in useful all-terrain form factors (seven-seat people movers, cargo haulers, and pickups). Those markets have no feasible second best alternative with Tesla Autonomy. We’re full believers in Optimus. When Tesla has units ready, we aim to build a line where humans and humanoids work coordinated shifts around the clock. This depends on attracting people who believe in the mission: extending the joy of this cutting-edge technology platform onto roads not yet traveled. Tesla has set the bar themselves for what a qualified operator looks like, and we intend to meet it. There is perhaps no company as loyal or committed to Tesla as UP. We’ve built on Tesla platforms since 2013, and we’d be honored to carry the torch. We’re grateful for the outpouring of support from Tesla owners and shareholders, and we look forward to continuing the discussion. For those looking to contribute: [email protected] — UP (@UnpluggedTesla) November 11, 2026

An Australian Army dozer embarks a Landing Craft Mechanized (LCM-8) at Cowley beach training area in Northern Queensland in preparation for Exercise Keris Woomera 2026. (Photo: Australian Department of Defence)
SINGAPORE — The Australian army’s recently created Littoral Manoeuvre Group is the correct move for the country’s armed forces, experts told Breaking Defense, especially as tensions continue in the Indo-Pacific.
Australia announced plans to transform its ground forces into a littoral-focused force in its 2024 National Defence Strategy , which called for an army “optimised for littoral manoeuvre with a long range land and maritime strike capability.”
In March, Australian Army established the Littoral Manoeuvre Group to strengthen the service’s “ability to move, deploy and support land forces across coastal and island regions.”
But as budget cuts to some programs loom to make room for AUKUS spending , experts warn that the unit needs to be adequately resourced to ensure it can fulfil that role.
In the wake of increased spending on commitments for the trilateral agreement, the country is conducting a budget review to free up funds for the acquisition of nuclear submarines, even as the country is pledging to bring defense spending up to three percent of its gross domestic product in the coming years.
Last month, the Littoral Manoeuvre Group completed a large-scale amphibious exercise during a training event with Indonesia.
John Blaxland, a professor of international security and intelligence studies at Australian National University, told Breaking Defense that an exercis e like that suggests that Australia envisages working with allies and partners to deploy forces to observe and safeguard key littoral sites, as well as control maritime chokepoints in a conflict.
“The Littoral Manoeuvre Group is a radical organisational design concept for Australia which reflects a significant reorientation towards being able to rapidly deploy and support forces operating over considerable distances alongside partners,” Blaxland said, adding that the group harks back to World War II, when Australian forces demonstrated mastery of combined arms warfare in the littorals.
Independent Australian naval commentator Alex Luck agreed, calling the focus on littoral operations “a step in the right direction.”
“Australia faces a difficult geographic challenge in its near abroad, in light of a rising Chinese military capability expanding into the wider Pacific and Indian Ocean theatres. Therefore the Australian Army will have to rely on significant naval mobility allowing for flexible coverage of maritime spaces including islands directly under Australian control and maritime approaches around Australian territory,” he added.
He also stressed the need to work with Australia’s neighbors and partners such as the US and New Zealand “in securing maritime features around Australia, but particularly across Pacific Island spaces.”
The Littoral Manoeuvre Group will include three landing craft battalions, each operating four medium and two heavy landing craft. Both Blaxland and Luck agree that outfitting the group with these landing craft is crucial.
Australia awarded contracts to Austal Australia for Land Craft Medium in December 2025 and for Landing Craft Heavy in February. LCM will have a cargo capacity of 80 tonnes (88 tons ) while the LCH will be able to transport 200 soldiers and six M1 Abrams tanks or nine Redback infantry vehicles.
Luck said the introduction of the two new classes of landing craft would introduce capabilities that the Australian Army has not operated in recent times.
“The LCH in particular, in conjunction with the Royal Australian Navy’s own amphibious assets, represents an unprecedented new resource the Australian Army will need time to further refine and develo p,” he said.
“It is therefore important to apply a step by step approach maturing these new amphibious capabilities to allow for further refinement, including allocation of additional resources further strengthening the new LMG concept,” he continued.
And while Australia’s plans to equip the new group as outlined in Australia’s defense Integrated Investment Program appear to be sufficient, Blaxland cautioned that those plans would take time to come to fruition and was dependent on whether funding is available to follow through.
“The plan appears to be to expand significantly to help move whole battalion groups and supporting elements to work alongside partner forces in the ‘littorals’ across the archipelago. But with significant funding constraints, this is not likely to reach full operational capacity for some years yet,” he said.

Tesla Roadster image: Tesla. Porsche Mission S image: Porsche
Tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche. Speaking at a conference in Berlin today, CEO Michael Leiters said Porsche wants “to completely steer clear from any kind of effects and shows,” according to Bloomberg .
Both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15. Tesla made a Roadster flip in mid-air. Porsche showed the Mission S, and Leiters says the two cars aren’t even chasing the same customers.
Thrusters vs. a supercar concept
Tesla finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype. The main event was a car using compressed-air thrusters to launch off a ramp, rotate in the air, and come back down on its wheels.
It was the payoff for months of hype. Musk spent most of the year promising a “flying” Roadster demo, and it slipped more than once. We reported in June that it had been pushed to August to make room for SpaceX thruster work.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
There are three versions. The Performance trim uses suction fans and claims 0-60 mph in under 1.6 seconds, the Thrust trim adds rear cold-gas thrusters for a claimed sub-0.9-second run, and the single-seat Rocket trim gets thrusters all around the car and isn’t approved for public roads. Tesla gave no price and no production date, just Musk’s “2028, actually.”
Porsche went the other way. Under the skin, the Mission S can take either a hybrid or a straight combustion powertrain. It’s a mid-engine car that sits above the 911 in the lineup, and well above it in price.
Leiters said customer response has been “overwhelming” and that Porsche would rather show off real technical innovation than put on a show. If it reaches production, Ferrari is the obvious target, and Porsche hasn’t played in that segment since the 918 Spyder. Porsche is counting on a pricier, more exclusive lineup to rebuild its profits.
Not everyone in the supercar world agrees with Leiters. Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna rated Tesla’s Roadster launch “10 out of 10” last month.
Electrek’s Take
Leiters has a point, even if Porsche pitching a gas and hybrid supercar as “technical innovation” in 2026 is a bit rich. But what bothers me more is who Tesla is aiming at.
I’m concerned Tesla is starting to appeal to the lowest common denominator: people who watch a Roadster hop off a ramp and believe an actual flying car is coming. Musk pushed that idea himself. On Joe Rogan’s show, he called the upcoming demo “unforgettable” and said that if Peter Thiel wants a flying car, “we should be able to buy one.”
That’s not real. Cold-gas thrusters work like a giant can of compressed air, and the math is brutal. The Rocket trim carries 400 liters of air at 10,000 psi, roughly 200 kg of gas. At the roughly 80 kN its rear thrusters produce, even a very efficient nozzle empties that tank in a few seconds. Then refilling it takes six to seven hours .

Dacia Sandero Will Get an Electric Variant for the First Time, Combustion Models Live On
6 photos
Photo: Dacia
The next-generation Dacia Sandero will have an all-electric variant for the first time. The electric powertrain will borrow parts from the Renault 5 E-Tech, although the Sandero will retain the current platform to accommodate combustion variants. These will include a new entry-level TCe engine and a more affordable full-hybrid powertrain.
European carmakers have been so focused on relaxing emissions regulations that they forgot to take car buyers into consideration. Happy to be allowed to sell combustion vehicles beyond 2035, they failed to notice the tectonic shift that was triggered by the Iran war and the rising fuel prices. As customers flocked to buy electric vehicles, legacy carmakers have few electric models in their lineups.
Dacia has been among the carmakers that were hit the hardest when European customers migrated en masse towards electric vehicles. The budget carmaker has only one electric model in its lineup, the Spring city car . Despite its attractive price and decent performance, the Dacia Spring is far from being able to address all transportation needs of European customers.
Thankfully, the budget carmaker in Renault's portfolio is already working on an electric variant of the Sandero, its most popular model. According to Autocar, the next-generation Dacia Sandero will offer in 2028 an electric powertrain for the first time. Production is scheduled to begin in Morocco in April 2028.
The next-generation Sandero will be fresh, but not entirely new. Autocar reports that Dacia will continue to use the current RGMP platform (previously known as CMF-B). Besides that, the upcoming model will retain the underlying body structure, including the roof, A-pillars, door structures, and glazing.
This has two important benefits. On the one hand, Dacia saves substantially in development costs and tooling at the Casablanca factory in Morocco. Secondly, Dacia can continue to build combustion variants of the Sandero without needing to redesign the platform. The downside is that the Sandero will adapt the RGMP platform to include a battery pack and electric drive unit, with all the negatives.
These crucial parts will be sourced from the Renault 5 E-Tech, including the 44-kWh LFP battery and the 107-hp electric motor. Since these components must be integrated into the ICE platform, expect a few rough edges, especially in terms of packaging and efficiency. The range is expected to hover around 400 km (250 miles), obviously according to the European WLTP standard.
Changes are also expected on the IVCE front. Renault will replace the entry-level 1.0-liter TCe engine with a new 1.2-liter variant still developing 99 hp. A more affordable full-hybrid powertrain is also anticipated, built around a 114-hp 1.2-liter TCe engine.
Even though the platform and bodywork stay largely unchanged, the next-generation Dacia Sandero will feature a complete redesign inspired by the Striker. The dashboard will also be new, with more upscale materials and a more attractive styling. Physical controls will be kept for important functions. Still, the center screen will gain more prominence as the human-machine interface.
