A Texas trucking company owner has been indicted on federal charges from an alleged scheme to employ unauthorized foreign drivers to transport domestic freight across the U.S., saving his company nearly $300,000 in labor costs.
Armando Martinez Varela, 56, of Laredo, Texas, owned VMS Transport LLC, which prosecutors allege recruited drivers admitted into the U.S. under B-1 nonimmigrant visa status to perform domestic trucking work they were not authorized to undertake.
VMS Transport LLC records allegedly showed that 57 B-1 visa drivers completed 1,044 domestic transportation trips between Feb. 20 and May 15, according to an announcement on Tuesday from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Texas.
The drivers picked up trailers in Laredo and delivered freight to destinations throughout the U.S., federal prosecutors said.
The indictment alleges Varela used the arrangement to substantially reduce the company’s labor expenses by paying the foreign drivers between 25 cents and 50 cents per mile, compared with approximately 70 cents per mile paid to authorized drivers performing similar work.
Federal authorities estimate the company saved approximately $299,606 in labor costs through the alleged arrangement.
Armando Martinez Varela, owner of Laredo-based VMS Transport LLC, is pictured with a Homeland Security Investigations agent. Varela faces federal charges stemming from an alleged scheme to employ unauthorized B-1 visa drivers to haul domestic freight across the United States. (Photo: U.S. Attorney’s Office, Southern District of Texas)
VMS Transport LLC is a Laredo-based interstate trucking company operating 53 power units and employing 50 drivers. Federal records show the carrier underwent 90 roadside inspections during the 24-month period ending Nov. 9, resulting in 12 driver out-of-service violations and 10 vehicle out-of-service violations. Its driver out-of-service rate of 13.3% was nearly double the national average of 6.67%.
VMS Transport was also involved in two reportable crashes during that period, including one involving injuries. FMCSA records listed the carrier’s operating authority as active as of Nov. 9.
The case comes amid heightened federal attention to immigration compliance and the use of foreign drivers in U.S. trucking operations, particularly along the southern border.
Federal authorities have increasingly scrutinized the use of B-1 visas in trucking operations , including whether drivers entering the U.S. for international transportation are performing unauthorized domestic freight movements.
Varela faces charges involving the employment of unauthorized workers, encouraging or inducing unlawful entry or residence, harboring unauthorized immigrants and making materially false statements to federal investigators.
If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in federal prison and a possible maximum fine of $250,000, according to prosecutors.
Under federal rules, qualifying B-1 drivers may participate in international freight movements but generally cannot transport cargo picked up at one U.S. location and delivered to another U.S. destination when the movement is entirely domestic.
Prosecutors allege Varela recruited B-1 visa holders specifically to haul domestic freight after picking up trailers in Laredo.
The indictment also alleges Varela arranged housing for the drivers between assignments rather than having them return to Mexico.
The Justice Department’s announcement did not specify whether additional company officials or drivers face charges in connection with the alleged scheme.
It also did not identify the freight customers involved or the destinations served by the 1,044 domestic transportation trips.
Why it matters: The indictment against Armando Martinez Varela, owner of VMS Transport LLC, highlights federal scrutiny of trucking companies accused of using improperly authorized foreign drivers to reduce labor costs and compete with compliant carriers.

KTM X-Bow Arrow to Sell for $99K, Throws in a 330-HP Audi Engine and 24 Inches of Suspension Travel
6 photos
Photo: KTM
It's been a long time since we last heard anything from KTM X-Bow, the offshoot of the namesake Austrian bike maker that is into making four-wheeled vehicles. Recently sold by the mother company to Dakar competitor Guillaume de Mévius and his crew, X-Bow quickly got to work, and it just presented this week its first-ever product as an independent company.
Make room for the X-Bow Arrow, the company's first-ever side-by-side and, at the same time, what is hoped to be the beginning of a new chapter for the brand. A vehicle that was designed by people used to taking on the roughest off-road courses on the planet, and packed to the teeth with high-end tech.
At the core of the four-wheeler is a chromoly steel chassis supported on all corners by double wishbone suspension and dedicated shocks manufactured with assistance from specialist KW Reiger.
The hardware is supposedly fit and ready to deliver some 23.6 inches (600 mm) of travel for the most demanding off-road courses to be easily overcome. Backing the suspension system are limited-slip differentials installed on both ends.
What gets the Arrow going is not some new powertrain designed in-house, but Audi's tried and tested EA888 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine. Why Audi? Well, the Germans have been involved with X-Bow one way or another for almost two decades now.
In this application, the powertrain is tied to a seven-speed DSG transmission and, depending on configuration (there will be a couple of them), two power levels will be on the table.
KTM X-Bow plans to first make both standard versions and limited editions of the vehicle. In its native, standard-spec form, the side-by-side's powertrain is rated at 280 horsepower, while the limited-edition variants will boost that to an impressive 330 hp.
The latter will also be equipped with a hydraulic fly-off handbrake, a fully enclosed cabin and standard air conditioning, and Sabelt premium seating and harness systems, among other yet-to-be-detailed things.
X-Bow says first-to-market will be the Arrow Black Limited Edition, which will be offered through an exclusive reservation period that opens on November 17, 2026. Just 500 of these things will be made, each priced at $98,600. That's right, a sum that's uncomfortably close to the six-digit territory. The standard KTM B-Bow Arrow, on the other hand, is valued at almost half that, $59,800.
We're told more details on both variants will be released closer to the official market entry of the revived X-Bow, including additional technical specifications, pricing, and availability details.
Naturally, we'll keep an eye on things and report back once we know more, but don't hold your breath for news in the near future: the company behind this project says first deliveries will not take place before late next year.

Latam Airlines Group announced Wednesday it will build and finance a new cargo terminal at El Dorado International Airport in Bogotá, Colombia, tripling its existing work space and enabling faster processing of import and export shipments.
The expansion project is part of a new plan to upgrade cargo handling infrastructure at its primary operating hubs.
The 46,400-square foot El Dorado facility will also allow Latam’s cargo division to expand cold storage capacity by about 20% to support the growth of the flower export market, where Latam says it already holds a 35% market share.
Latam Cargo also said it plans to expand its domestic cargo facilities in Bogotá and establish a new space dedicated to handling the growing inflow of imported cargo.
“This investment is essential to leverage the airline’s future growth plans in the Colombian market and represents a renewed vote of confidence by LATAM Group in the country,” said Santiago Álvarez, chief commercial officer of Latam Cargo, in a news release.
Why It Matters: Latam is the largest airline in South America and its freighter division operates 19 Boeing 767-300 converted cargo jets.
Latam has also made improvements at three regional airports in Colombia to more efficiently transfer cargo carried on passenger flights. The enhancements inluce expanding warehouse space, upgrading X-ray screening equipment and implement new counter technologies to expedite cargo acceptance and drop-off.
More broadly, Latam is striving to digitize end-to-end data exchange with industry stakeholders and customs authorities to improve service and efficiency.
The physical expansion is coupled with a digital transformation strategy. In Colombia specifically, it has deployed artificial intelligence and RFID-based tracking tools for flower shipments, complemented by the CargoLink platform for advance cargo acceptance.
Virtual reality warehouse training
Last month, Latam Cargo revealed the deployment of virtual reality technology for training warehouse personnel at its Miami hub. The initiative strengthens operational safety by allowing teams to practice, manage, and respond to real-time scenarios within a controlled digital environment.
In its initial phase, the custom-designed program will cover about 550 employees, including 250 forklift operators. Unlike conventional training methods, the immersive platform captures precise behavioral metrics, including contingency response times as well as the immediate identification and mitigation of hazards.
To ensure complete operational realism, the simulators — co-developed with LATAM Group’s internal training arm, Academia LATAM — feature scenarios across six warehouse pedestrian zones and three specialized modules for forklift drivers. During training, personnel navigate high-risk procedures such as dangerous goods segregation, cargo handling, pedestrian traffic flow, and machinery separation protocol, boosting their overall situational awareness.
Following an initial rollout for onboarding training at the Fast Air warehouse in Santiago, Chile, the Miami launch marks a major scale-up, adding broader operational scenarios.
Latam said it is currently assessing the expansion of this VR training system to other strategic hubs, including in Brazil.
